subject: Unable to get coef(IRTparams=T) for multidimensional model + plotting ICCs.

messages.author: 77967791f3032708
messages.subject: Unable to get coef(IRTparams=T) for multidimensional model + plotting ICCs.
parts:
Hello all,

  • how come mirt is not capable of acquiring true IRT parameters (discrimination and difficulty) when using coef() for multidimensional model? And is it possible to recalculate intercept to difficulty parameter via formula 

           intercept = -discrimination*difficulty  (If yes, I cannot see why the package would'nt be capable of that.)  ?

          And does the above formula work even for 3PL model?
  • Is it possible for mirt to plot ICC curves in a plane? What I mean by that is, I have 3 dimensional model and I want to plot ICC curves for each factor's item. What I get from 
    itemplot(model,type='trace',item=1) is 23 3D plots and I really cannot interpret anything from these. My tip is, since my model is 3 dimensional, plot is also 3D and each axis represent one factor. I would like to see the plot in the same manner I get it from plot(...) for unidimensional model. Is it possible?
      This is what I get when I add to the itemplot: facet_items=T:


With any kind of help I would be really grateful (+ I am already grateful to the author of the package).

VH

That's for unidimensional models. What do you suppose the difficulty parameters look like for multidimensional models, which are intended to reflect the inflection locations on the probability surfaces?

It shouldn't be model specific.

    itemplot(model,type='trace',item=1) is 23 3D plots and I really cannot interpret anything from these. My tip is, since my model is 3 dimensional, plot is also 3D and each axis represent one factor. I would like to see the plot in the same manner I get it from plot(...) for unidimensional model. Is it possible?
      This is what I get when I add to the itemplot: facet_items=T:


With any kind of help I would be really grateful (+ I am already grateful to the author of the package).

These are admittedly ugly, but visualizing 4D spaces is difficult anway (it's not a 3 dimensional model, it's four; three traits + the ordinate dimension, which in this case is the probability value). I don't have great suggestions for a fix, but I'm open to suggestions.

Phil

 

VH

Dear Phil,

what exactly do you mean with

That's for unidimensional models. What do you suppose the difficulty parameters look like for multidimensional models, which are intended to reflect the inflection locations on the probability surfaces?

Somehow I couldn't read between the lines. You didn't deny the recalculation between intercept and the difficulty parameter. Are you implying that for multidimensional model it is not common to report difficulty parameters?

As for the 3D plot, my mistake, I didn't realize it's actually 4D. Nonetheless, is there a possibility to plot P(theta_1), ..., P(theta_n) in 2D as curve despite there are more dimensions in the model? Just in case I am interested in the relationship for 1 factor separately (2D curve), not for the whole test, where of course is better to see the whole surface (for 2 dimensions). 

Another question - how do you explore the results for more ten 2 or 3 dimensions? It's not graphically reproducable, then what to extract from the results (only coef() function's results?) ? And is it possible to get I_i(theta_1,..., theta_n) the item information function and also the total one? So far for simple models I created my own python script to extract from intercept, slope and guessing all the functions including standard error measure, so I was curious whether I can get those results from mirt directly.

Thank you very much, Phil.

VH

messages.subject: Re: Unable to get coef(IRTparams=T) for multidimensional model + plotting ICCs.
parts:
On Mon, Jun 15, 2020 at 8:51 PM Václav Homola <vaclav.h...@gmail.com> wrote:
Dear Phil,

what exactly do you mean with 

That's for unidimensional models. What do you suppose the difficulty parameters look like for multidimensional models, which are intended to reflect the inflection locations on the probability surfaces?

Somehow I couldn't read between the lines. You didn't deny the recalculation between intercept and the difficulty parameter. Are you implying that for multidimensional model it is not common to report difficulty parameters?

There is no single difficulty parameter in multidimensional models; they represent vectors of locations across the probability space, and therefore there are an infinite number of them (in a 3D surface plot with the 2PLM, think how many possible combinations could result in P(theta1_theta2) = .5, for example)

As for the 3D plot, my mistake, I didn't realize it's actually 4D. Nonetheless, is there a possibility to plot P(theta_1), ..., P(theta_n) in 2D as curve despite there are more dimensions in the model? Just in case I am interested in the relationship for 1 factor separately (2D curve), not for the whole test, where of course is better to see the whole surface (for 2 dimensions).

No, this is a curse of dimensionality. If you're lucky to have some 0 cross-loadings for a given item the itemplot() function has a drop.zeros argument to reduce the dimensionality of a given item, but for the overall test the number of dimensions cannot be reduced without marginalizing information.

Another question - how do you explore the results for more ten 2 or 3 dimensions? It's not graphically reproducable, then what to extract from the results (only coef() function's results?) ? And is it possible to get I_i(theta_1,..., theta_n) the item information function and also the total one? So far for simple models I created my own python script to extract from intercept, slope and guessing all the functions including standard error measure, so I was curious whether I can get those results from mirt directly.

I think you just have to become more comfortable with the mathematical aspects of the models for higher dimensional tests, as you're correct visualization starts to fail. Similar problems happen in all multidimensional modeling methods (e.g., think structural equation modeling and why response surfaces are never visualized in that framework). HTH.

Phil

Thank you very much, Phil.

VH
